title: She Is Twenty. She Is Second. And She Has White Against the Leader. Divya Deshmukh's Norway Chess Title Charge Is Now or Never.
excerpt: Divya Deshmukh faces tournament leader Bibisara Assaubayeva with the white pieces in Round 8. A classical win would blow the women's title race wide open with two rounds to play.
body:
Divya Deshmukh has waited seven rounds for this. On Tuesday in Oslo, the twenty-year-old Indian Grandmaster will sit across from Kazakhstan's Bibisara Assaubayeva — the tournament leader — with the white pieces and everything on the line.

After Round 7, Assaubayeva leads the Norway Chess Women's event with 12.5 points. Divya is second on 10. Anna Muzychuk sits third at 9.5, close enough to pounce. But only Divya has a head-to-head match against the leader in this critical stretch, and she has the colour advantage.

## Why This Round Matters

In Norway Chess's unique format — classical games plus armageddon tiebreakers — a classical win is worth three points. If Divya beats Assaubayeva in classical play, the gap shrinks from 2.5 to just half a point with two rounds remaining. If she draws and wins the armageddon, the deficit narrows to one point. But if she loses — even in armageddon — the title effectively slips away.

The stakes could not be clearer.

## Divya's Tournament So Far

Divya entered Norway Chess as the youngest competitor in either the Open or Women's field, but she has played with the composure of a veteran. In Round 7, she drew the classical game against the experienced Koneru Humpy and then won the armageddon tiebreaker with the black pieces — a result that required both nerve and precision.

Her tournament has been a study in resilience. A painful Round 6 saw her lose to former Women's World Champion Ju Wenjun in classical play, a setback that could have derailed her campaign. Instead, she has won armageddon in three of her last four rounds, grinding out points even when classical victories proved elusive.

"Divya once again showed great fighting spirit," noted RevSportz in their Round 6 report, even after the loss to Ju. That spirit has been the defining feature of her Oslo campaign.

## The Assaubayeva Factor

Bibisara Assaubayeva, 22, has been the player to beat all tournament. Her Round 7 classical victory over China's Zhu Jiner — a controlled, technically assured win — gave her a commanding 12.5 points and breathing room at the top. The Kazakh star has lost only one classical game in the event and has been ruthlessly efficient in armageddon.

But Assaubayeva has not yet faced Divya with Black. The Indian's preparation with White will be crucial — and there is recent history to draw on. Both players competed in the 2026 Candidates Tournament, where Divya finished seventh and Assaubayeva was not in the field. Divya's experience at the highest level of competitive chess has deepened considerably this year.

## The Broader Indian Story

The Norway Chess Open section has its own Indian drama. After Round 7, Wesley So leads with 12.5 points, but Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa — who beat Alireza Firouzja in classical play — sits at 9 points, tied with Magnus Carlsen and Vincent Keymer. World Champion D. Gukesh is at 8 points after drawing classically with So but winning the armageddon.

Three Indian players competing at this level simultaneously — Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa, and Divya — would have been unimaginable a decade ago. Today it is simply the state of Indian chess.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRI chess fans following the action from North America and the UK, the timing is forgiving. Norway Chess streams begin in the late morning Eastern time, and the women's section has provided some of the most dramatic moments of the tournament.

Divya's rise also carries significance beyond the board. Her family relocated from Nagpur to support her chess career, enduring financial strain and years of early-morning training. A strong finish in Norway would cement her status as the leading Indian woman in chess and boost her case ahead of a potential Women's World Championship challenge.

## What Comes Next

Vaishali Rameshbabu won the Women's Candidates earlier this year and will challenge Ju Wenjun for the Women's World Championship title later in 2026. But Divya's trajectory suggests she will be next in line. A title challenge in Norway, or even a strong runner-up finish, would announce her arrival at the summit of women's chess.

Round 8 is scheduled for Tuesday, June 3. For Divya Deshmukh, it is the biggest game of her career so far.
